entry.title: MinTRL: How Long a Track Record Do You Actually Need?
entry.summary: A Sharpe ratio of 2.0 on 18 months of data proves almost nothing. Minimum Track Record Length turns “impressive Sharpe” into “how many years would this take to believe” — with the numbers. A strategy shows a Sharpe ratio of 2.0. Your instinct says “excellent.” The correct response is a question: over how long? Minimum Track Record Length (MinTRL) is the answer to that question, formalised. It asks: given an observed Sharpe ratio, how many years of track record would you need before you could believe, with 95% confidence, that the true Sharpe is above zero — that the strategy is better than nothing at all? entry.title: JWT verifiers need an explicit token-purpose policy
entry.summary:
JWT verifiers need an explicit token-purpose policy
A JSON Web Token can carry a request, a session, an access grant, a logout event, or a signed claim from an external service. If a verifier accepts all of them through the same key and the same parser, the token's header becomes a hint rather than a security control. RFC 8725 recommends explicit typing for this reason, and RFC 9068 gives OAuth access tokens a concrete type value that resource servers can enforce. The algorithm field is another decision point. The token header names an algorithm, but the verifier must choose the acceptable key type and algorithm from its own configuration. Trusting a kid to select any key in a shared set, or trusting alg to select a key type without an allowlist, expands the attack surface across every t…

entry.title: WordPress Core flaw: interpreting 62.969 blocked attack attempts
entry.summary: Wordfence reported blocking 62.969 attack attempts in 24 hours targeting a WordPress Core vulnerability. This measures attempts Wordfence says it blocked, not successfully compromised websites. The cited data does not establish an exploitation success rate. The vulnerability affects WordPress Core versions 4.7 through 7.1.3, has a CVSS score of 8,1, and has no CVE identifier. A patch was released on 28 October 2026. TMGS recommends updating affected installations to 7.1.4. During a Core update using a full package, affected versions extract files into a predictable directory under wp-content/upgrade. On many servers, this staging area is accessible through the web. An unauthenticated attacker reaching it at the right moment could interact with the staged WordPress installation and progress to PHP code execution on the server. Wordfence emphasizes that successful exploitation requires hitting a very narrow window while the full Core update is being extracted. That condition limits what can be inferred from the attempt count. TMGS assesses that the short window does not justify lowering remediation priority when attack attempts have already appeared. TMGS recommends inventorying WordPress websites, identifying affected versions, and prioritizing updates to 7.1.4. Prepare backups, recovery options, and post-update operational checks. TMGS also recommends: Verify the running version after updating and record it in the asset inventory. Review suspicious requests to PHP files under wp-content/upgrade, focusing on activity before, during, and after the upgrade. Correlate requests with error logs and file changes before concluding that a compromise occurred. For outsourced website management, assign clear responsibilities across content administrators, hosting providers, and security teams. Record the final version, upgrade time, and contact responsible for access logs. Read the full analysis on TMGS: https://tmgs.vn/tin-tuc/wordpress-doc-dung-62-969-luot-tan-cong-bi-chan-i.d487a618-e176-4ef5-b74a-5dd1345f7d37
